_comment: An e2e fixture for #794 (the ground's phase lag), not a world anyone plays.
Three bodies. Meridian and Afternoon are the pair: what the printed temperature columns read
is their surface block -- the stated anchor, the even share, and the absence or presence of
lag_tau -- and on those columns exactly one key differs, so the difference between their
pictures can only be the lag. Their RAILS are not identical (different distance, different
orbital rate, different seed), and that is harmless only because the anchor is STATED rather
than derived from the orbit: no printed kelvin reads the rail, so a case pins arithmetic
instead of bounding an orbit.
That stated anchor is the whole trick. A derived anchor puts the sun's distance into every
number and the case would be pinning where a body happens to sit, not what its ground does.
AltoFrio is the same knob on a body that ALSO has a height term: an air that lapses, so its
palette has to price mountains and a lag at once. That pairing is where a lagged palette is
easiest to get wrong, because the darkest light and the tallest ground are not the same place
on a lagged world -- and a palette priced from the two extremes separately leaves colours in
the legend that no pixel ever wears.
Balmy and Sultry are a second pair for the other readers of the ground: a hull flying in air
that follows its ground (#724 rung D). Both author air_follow, both have a flat profile -- no
lapse, so no height term anywhere -- and only Sultry authors lag_tau. They share one rail
(0.00015 rad/s, 0.9 rad apart on it) and one 21,549 s spin, which makes their SOLAR day
44,375 s -- the orbital rate is about half the spin rate, so the star walks round a little
slower than the ground turns. One radian of phase is 7,064 s of that day, and a case window of
~50 s of sim never sees it elapse; it does not need to. At tau 1 the lag alone is worth 53 K
with the sun 71 deg up, so one instant carries the whole disagreement. What the close rail
buys is light (1.81e6 W/m2) and an air shell thick enough for a cruise bed to sit in.
Sultry's rail is also inclined (orb_incl 0.5, lon_asc_node 0.9) while Balmy's is flat. That
is the frame pin: the log has to solve the lag in the body's SPINNING axes, and the wrong way
to get there is invisible on a rail whose orientation is the identity -- measured +5.4 K on
Sultry's underfoot column, and a 0.6 K break in the row's own air closure, against 0.00 K on
Balmy. It also gives the lagged one a real declination, so its day arc is not the flat 180.
Tilt: 0.05 rad on the pair, which means a near-zero season -- the declination stays within
about 1e-5 rad of the equator for the whole window a case runs, so the tilted-star branch of
the row model is NOT what those two cases exercise. AltoFrio carries a real 23.44 deg AND a
deliberately short 1047 s year, so a case that runs ~1100 s of sim around it watches the
declination sweep a whole season: that is where the tilted star's asymmetric day arc (the
kset/crise endpoints that are NOT the atan(tau) textbook shift) gets driven end to end.
Nothing in the shipped corpus authors a lag: until a real body gets one, every world on
screen still tracks the light exactly (tau absent = the sentinel = the unlagged law).

surface.temperature_src: INVENTED: a fixture's stated ground, so the anchor sits on the STATED rung and no rail enters the numbers
surface.even_share_src: INVENTED: near-bare-rock knob (the airless swing is wide on purpose, so a lag moves the picture by tens of kelvin rather than by a rounding hair)
surface._lag_comment: No lag_tau here on purpose: this body is the control. Absence is the sentinel, not a 0.0 a file wrote.

surface.temperature_src: INVENTED: same as Meridian's, so the two bodies' swings start from one anchor
surface.even_share_src: INVENTED: same knob as Meridian's -- the lag and the even share both set amplitude, so a lagged body needs its f re-fit before it ships for real (#794 step 5)
surface.lag_tau_src: INVENTED: one radian of PHASE (not hours; the loader takes any tau up to authored.h's kLagTauMaxPhase but demands a lag_tau_src beside every active one, which is what stops a file quietly authoring a day here). In time it is tau / the synodic rate = 1 / 2.9115e-4 = 3435 s against this body's 21580 s solar day -- about ONE SIXTH of a day, not a third; an author who scales tau from a stated 'peak at 14:00' should read that ratio, not guess. It puts the hottest ground ~40 deg east of the subsolar meridian and lifts the night floor, which is what the case pins.

surface.temperature_src: INVENTED: the fixture's stated ground again, so the anchor stays off the rail even with an air on the body
surface.even_share_src: INVENTED: same near-bare-rock knob as the pair, so the lag's effect on the palette is the same size here and the ONLY new thing is a height term
surface.lag_tau_src: INVENTED: same one radian of phase as Afternoon's -- this body exists to ask what happens when that knob meets a lapse profile, not to try a second lag value

atmosphere._relief_comment: The 6.5 K/km is Earth's, chosen because it is the value the #793 relief tests already reason about. It is NOT this body's climate: with a 240 K anchor the ground is far colder than the 288 K this layer's datum states, and the fixture does not care -- relief enters as a height term outside the fourth-power bracket, so the profile's own base temperature never meets the ground's. The 70 km top is NOT Earth's 85 km either: on the 9.81 m/s^2 this mass and radius pull with, this profile is down to 10 Pa by ~75 km, and #682's check refuses a shell whose ceiling floats in vacuum.

surface.temperature_src: INVENTED: the fixture's stated ground again, so the anchor stays off the rail even with an air on the body
surface.even_share_src: INVENTED: the same near-bare-rock knob as the pair, so the two bodies' swings are one swing
_air_comment: The air is here for #724 rung D: with air_follow authored, the kelvin a hull flies
through is the profile moved toward the ground under it, which is the coupling the
flight log's own air_T / prof_T / w / follow columns close on.
No lapse on purpose. A profile that cools with height gives the ground a height term
(#793), and then the log's underfoot_T carries a term a case cannot reprice from the
row -- it would have to know the terrain under the hull. With a flat profile the
coupling's ground is anchor-plus-forcing and nothing else, so the arithmetic in the
case is the arithmetic in the law.
The 210 K datum sits BELOW this body's 240 K anchor so the ground is the warmer of the
two by day and the air reads above its profile. It is not a climate claim.

atmosphere._air_follow_comment: 0.350 is the same value Kerbin carries (#724 rung D), so the two bodies' coupling has one strength. Not a _src key: the loader reads provenance for temperature, albedo, even_share and lag_tau only, so a note here is a note and nothing refuses a stale one.

surface.temperature_src: INVENTED: Balmy's anchor, so the two bodies differ by their lag and nothing else
surface.lag_tau_src: INVENTED: one radian of phase, as Afternoon's. In TIME this body pays 1 / 1.4157e-4 = 7,064 s of a 44,375 s solar day, which no ~50 s case window can watch elapse -- the disagreement shows up as 53 K at one instant with the sun 71 deg up, not as a lagged afternoon in the rows.

atmosphere._air_follow_comment: Balmy's 0.350, deliberately identical: the only difference between the two bodies' flight logs is the lag.
